)

FROM t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY Region, rn;

title: Monthly rank of regions

WITH m AS (
    SELECT MONTH(e.ProductionDate) AS MonthNo, p.Region, SUM(e.PlannedCost) AS Total,

    JOIN retail_manufacturing.Products AS p ON p.ProductID = e.ProductID
    GROUP BY MONTH(e.ProductionDate), p.Region

FROM m

ORDER BY MonthNo;

title: Repeat production orders within N days
q: Find production orders that happened within @Days days of the same product's previous production order. Use @Days = 145. Show product, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT ProductID, ProductionOrderID, ProductionDate,
           LAG(ProductionDate) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductID ORDER BY ProductionDate, ProductionOrderID) AS PrevDate
    FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders
)
SELECT ProductID, PrevDate, ProductionDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, ProductionDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, ProductionDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY ProductID, ProductionDate;
how: LAG finds the previous production order and DATEDIFF measures the gap. A variable makes the window easy to change. Repeat-activity checks like this are a common interview question.

SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS TableName,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'PK' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS PK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'F'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'UQ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UQ,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'C'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'D'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DF
FROM sys.objects
WHERE type IN ('PK', 'F', 'UQ', 'C', 'D')
  AND SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) = 'retail_manufacturing'
GROUP BY parent_object_id
ORDER BY TableName;
how: Prefer declarative constraints: they are faster, always applied, and help the optimizer. Use triggers only for cross-table rules, and application checks for friendly messages.

title: Production order chain for one product
q: Starting from product 1's first production order, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that product's production orders in date order, with a step number.
sql:
WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT ProductionOrderID, ProductionDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ProductionDate, ProductionOrderID) AS rn
    FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders
    WHERE ProductID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT ProductionOrderID, ProductionDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.ProductionOrderID, o.ProductionDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1
    FROM Ordered AS o
    JOIN Chain AS c ON o.rn = c.rn + 1
)
SELECT ProductionOrderID, ProductionDate, Step
FROM Chain
ORDER BY Step;
how: The anchor picks the starting row. The recursive part finds the next row (rn + 1) one step at a time. The same shape walks hierarchies such as org charts or bills of materials.

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)

title: Month-over-month with a calendar
q: For all 12 months of 2024 (even empty ones), show total planned cost, previous month's total and growth %.

WITH Months AS (
    SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS date) AS m
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(month, 1, m) FROM Months WHERE m < '2024-12-01'
), Totals AS (
    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.PlannedCost), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e
           ON e.ProductionDate >= mo.m AND e.ProductionDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)
    GROUP BY mo.m
)
SELECT m AS MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))
            / NULLIF(LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0) AS decimal(6,1)) AS GrowthPct

ORDER BY m;

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > product) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.
sql:
DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM retail_manufacturing.Products
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.ProductID, r.NodeID, p.ProductName
FROM retail_manufacturing.Products AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.ProductID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

q: Sync material prices from a staging list: update prices that changed, insert new materials, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (MaterialID int, MaterialName nvarchar(80), MaterialCode varchar(20), UnitCost decimal(12,2));
INSERT INTO @Stage VALUES
    (1,  N'Acetaminophen 325mg tablet', 'MAT-00001', 0.09),   -- price change
    (2,  N'Acetaminophen 500mg tablet', 'MAT-00002', 0.10),   -- no change
    (51, N'Loratadine 10mg tablet',     'MAT-00051', 0.12);   -- new

MERGE retail_manufacturing.Materials AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.MaterialID = s.MaterialID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.UnitCost <> s.UnitCost THEN
    UPDATE SET t.UnitCost = s.UnitCost
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (MaterialID, MaterialName, MaterialCode, UnitCost)
    VALUES (s.MaterialID, s.MaterialName, s.MaterialCode, s.UnitCost)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.MaterialID, deleted.UnitCost AS OldCost, inserted.UnitCost AS NewCost;

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = @@SPID;
how: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED (the default) prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantom rows. title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each product's total production order planned cost and total number of material usage records. Make sure the planned cost is not double counted.
sql:

       ISNULL(ch.TotalPlannedCost, 0) AS TotalPlannedCost,
       ISNULL(li.MaterialUsage, 0) AS MaterialUsage
FROM retail_manufacturing.Products AS p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT ProductID, SUM(PlannedCost) AS TotalPlannedCost
           FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders
           GROUP BY ProductID) AS ch ON ch.ProductID = p.ProductID
LEFT JOIN (SELECT e.ProductID, COUNT(*) AS MaterialUsage
           FROM retail_manufacturing.MaterialUsage AS r

title: Short-circuit is not guaranteed
q: Return materials where the name has a space and the text before the first space is longer than 8 characters. Write it safely so CHARINDEX never gives a negative length.
sql:
SELECT MaterialName
FROM retail_manufacturing.Materials
WHERE CASE WHEN CHARINDEX(' ', MaterialName) > 0
           THEN LEN(LEFT(MaterialName, CHARINDEX(' ', MaterialName) - 1))
           ELSE 0
      END > 8;
how: SQL Server does not promise to evaluate AND conditions left to right, so `CHARINDEX(...) > 0 AND LEN(LEFT(... - 1)) > 8` could still error on a row with no space. A CASE expression controls the order. This is a senior-level detail.

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find production orders that are not a parent of any other production order, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).

SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e
   WHERE e.ProductionOrderID NOT IN (SELECT ParentProductionOrderID
                               FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentProductionOrderID = e.ProductionOrderID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentProductionOrderID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. title: Rank without window functions
q: Rank materials by unit cost (1 = most expensive) using a correlated subquery instead of RANK().
sql:
SELECT m.MaterialName, m.UnitCost,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_manufacturing.Materials AS x
        WHERE x.UnitCost > m.UnitCost) + 1 AS CostRank
FROM retail_manufacturing.Materials AS m
ORDER BY CostRank, m.MaterialName;
how: A row's rank is 1 + the number of rows with a higher cost. That gives the same result as RANK(), ties included.

title: Top product per region
q: Using only subqueries (no window functions), show the product with the highest total planned cost in each region.
sql:
SELECT t.Region, t.ProductName, t.Total
FROM (SELECT p.Region, p.ProductName, SUM(e.PlannedCost) AS Total
      FROM retail_manufacturing.Products AS p
      JOIN retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e ON e.ProductID = p.ProductID
      GROUP BY p.Region, p.ProductID, p.ProductName) AS t
WHERE t.Total = (SELECT MAX(t2.Total)
                 FROM (SELECT p2.Region, SUM(e2.PlannedCost) AS Total
                       FROM retail_manufacturing.Products AS p2
                       JOIN retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e2 ON e2.ProductID = p2.ProductID
                       GROUP BY p2.Region, p2.ProductID) AS t2
                 WHERE t2.Region = t.Region)
ORDER BY t.Region;

title: Production orders after a product's first material usage record
q: For each product who has a material usage record, count how many of their production orders happened after the production order of their first material usage record.
sql:
SELECT x.ProductID, COUNT(e.ProductionOrderID) AS LaterProductionOrders
FROM (SELECT e1.ProductID, MIN(e1.ProductionDate) AS FirstRxDate
      FROM retail_manufacturing.MaterialUsage AS li
      JOIN retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e1 ON e1.ProductionOrderID = li.ProductionOrderID
      GROUP BY e1.ProductID) AS x
LEFT JOIN retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e
       ON e.ProductID = x.ProductID
      AND e.ProductionDate > x.FirstRxDate
GROUP BY x.ProductID
ORDER BY LaterProductionOrders DESC, x.ProductID;

title: IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN
q: Return products with at least one Pending production order three ways (IN, EXISTS, JOIN with DISTINCT). Each should return the same count.
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_manufacturing.Products
   WHERE ProductID IN (SELECT ProductID FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders
                       WHERE Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaIn,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_manufacturing.Products AS p
   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e
                 WHERE e.ProductID = p.ProductID AND e.Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaExists,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.ProductID)
   FROM retail_manufacturing.Products AS p
   JOIN retail_manufacturing.ProductionOrders AS e ON e.ProductID = p.ProductID
   WHERE e.Status = 'Pending') AS ViaJoin;
how: All three give the same answer. A plain JOIN repeats a product for each matching production order, which is why DISTINCT is needed. IN and EXISTS never duplicate rows.

title: Materials priced above their group's average
q: Materials come in families (the first word of the name, e.g. 'Ibuprofen'). List materials that cost more than the average of their own family.
sql:
SELECT m.MaterialName, m.UnitCost
FROM retail_manufacturing.Materials AS m
WHERE m.UnitCost > (SELECT AVG(x.UnitCost)
                    FROM retail_manufacturing.Materials AS x
                    WHERE LEFT(x.MaterialName, CHARINDEX(' ', x.MaterialName) - 1)
                        = LEFT(m.MaterialName, CHARINDEX(' ', m.MaterialName) - 1))
ORDER BY m.MaterialName;
how: The family is computed with LEFT + CHARINDEX (text before the first space). The correlated subquery averages only materials of the same family.
